entries.meaning: Adds VLAN identification information to Ethernet frames on trunk links so one physical link can carry traffic for multiple VLANs.
Controls access at a wired or wireless network edge by requiring authentication before ordinary traffic is permitted.
A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
A framework that verifies identity, decides permitted actions, and records activity.
A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.
A set of rules that permits or denies access to a resource, network path, or object.
An IPsec component that provides integrity and origin authentication without encrypting the payload.
A wireless device that connects Wi-Fi clients to a wired or distributed network.
A defined way for software components or services to exchange requests and data.
Windows terminology for automatic IPv4 link-local addressing in 169.254.0.0/16 when a client cannot obtain a normal DHCP lease.
A protocol that maps an IPv4 address to a local network hardware address.
A policy that defines permitted and prohibited use of organizational systems and data.
The routing protocol used to exchange reachability information between autonomous systems on the internet.
A twist-lock coaxial connector found in legacy networking, video, and test equipment.
A Spanning Tree Protocol message that switches exchange to elect a root bridge, calculate topology information, and detect changes.
The identifier for one wireless basic service set, commonly the MAC address of a specific access-point radio.
A model that permits personally owned devices to access organizational resources.
The switch memory table that associates learned MAC addresses with ports and VLANs for frame forwarding.
A distributed group of servers that places content closer to users to reduce latency and origin-server load.
A Cisco discovery protocol that advertises neighboring device identity and interface information on the local link.
Three foundational security goals: prevent unauthorized disclosure, preserve trustworthy data, and keep services usable.
Prefix-length notation and route aggregation that describe networks without relying on legacy address classes.
A text-based interface used to enter commands and inspect device or operating-system output.
A DNS alias record that points one name to another canonical hostname rather than directly to an address.
The processor that executes instructions. High utilization can affect control-plane work, services, or device responsiveness.
An error-detection value checked on received frames. Rising CRC errors often point to cabling, interference, optic, or duplex problems.
A short twinaxial copper cable assembly with integrated transceiver ends, commonly used for nearby high-speed switch or server connections.
Storage attached directly to one host rather than accessed through a file or storage network.
Connectivity between data centers, often carrying routed traffic or extended logical networks between sites.
A denial-of-service attack launched from many systems at once to exhaust a target's resources.
A protocol that automatically assigns IP configuration to network clients.
Controls that identify sensitive information and restrict unauthorized transfer or exposure.
A traditional term for an isolated network segment used for systems that need controlled exposure to less-trusted networks. Modern materials may call this a screened subnet.
The distributed service that maps names to records such as IP addresses and mail servers.
Extensions that add signed DNS data so resolvers can validate integrity and origin.
Carries DNS queries inside HTTPS, protecting the resolver traffic from simple observation or modification in transit.
An attack or condition that prevents legitimate users from accessing a service.
Carries DNS queries over a dedicated TLS-protected transport, normally TCP port 853.
Planning and technical arrangements used to restore systems, data, and services after a disruptive event.
The local-link framing used to carry 802.1X authentication messages between a supplicant and an authenticator.
A dynamic interior routing protocol that selects paths using a composite metric and exchanges routes within an organization.
The point when a product reaches the end of its planned life cycle. Availability, updates, and replacement planning may change.
The point when a vendor stops providing some or all support, fixes, or updates for a product or release.
An IPsec component that can provide encryption, integrity, and authentication for network traffic.
The wireless network name shared by multiple access points so users can move between them while staying on the same wireless network.
A contract that defines how software may be installed, used, and distributed.
A high-speed storage networking technology commonly used to carry block-storage traffic in a SAN.
A family of gateway-redundancy protocols that presents a virtual default-gateway address backed by multiple routers.
A legacy file-transfer protocol that does not encrypt credentials or content by default.
A European Union privacy regulation governing personal-data processing and individual rights.
A tunneling protocol that encapsulates one network-layer packet inside another but does not provide encryption by itself.
A graphical interface used to configure or monitor a system through windows, forms, menus, and visual controls.
The application protocol used for web requests and responses without built-in transport encryption.
HTTP protected by TLS to provide encrypted and authenticated transport.
A cloud model in which the provider supplies infrastructure while the customer manages operating systems, applications, and much of the configuration.
The management of infrastructure through versioned, repeatable configuration files or templates.
Processes and technologies for creating identities, authenticating users, and controlling access.
A network protocol used for diagnostics and control messages, including many ping and error responses.

entries.expansion: Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6
entries.meaning: IPv6 control messaging used for errors, diagnostics, neighbor discovery, router discovery, and other essential IPv6 functions.
Technology used to monitor and control industrial processes and physical equipment.
A local telecommunications room that distributes cabling and network access within part of a building and normally uplinks to the MDF.
A control that identifies suspicious activity and generates alerts without necessarily blocking traffic.

entries.expansion: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
entries.meaning: A professional standards organization responsible for many networking standards, including the IEEE 802 family used by Ethernet and wireless LAN technologies.
Connected industrial sensors, controllers, and equipment whose availability, safety, and long service life affect network design.
A protocol used to negotiate security associations and keys for IPsec.
Network-connected devices that sense, process, or control physical environments, often with limited resources and long lifecycles.
The network-layer protocol used to address and route packets between systems.
A system for tracking IP networks, addresses, assignments, reservations, DNS relationships, and address-space usage.
A standardized method for exporting metadata about network flows so collectors can analyze conversations, volume, endpoints, and timing without storing full packet payloads.
A control placed inline to detect and block suspicious traffic.
A suite of protocols that protects IP traffic through authentication, integrity, and optional encryption.
The 32-bit Internet Protocol address format written as four decimal octets, such as 192.0.2.10.
The 128-bit Internet Protocol address format designed for a much larger address space and modern autoconfiguration behavior.
A link-state interior routing protocol that exchanges topology information and calculates shortest paths within an autonomous system.
The standards-based protocol used to negotiate and maintain compatible links inside an Ethernet link-aggregation group.
A network covering a limited area such as an office, home, or campus segment.
A small fiber-optic connector commonly used on modern transceivers and patch panels.
A protocol used to query and manage directory services.

entries.expansion: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over TLS
entries.meaning: LDAP protected by TLS, commonly associated with TCP port 636. Modern deployments may also use LDAP with StartTLS.
A vendor-neutral local-link discovery protocol that advertises device, interface, VLAN, power, and other neighbor information.
The data-link layer function and hardware addressing used on local networks.
The main telecommunications room where external services, backbone cabling, and major distribution connections commonly meet.
An Ethernet port wiring arrangement that swaps transmit and receive pairs. Auto MDI-X lets modern ports correct this automatically.
Authentication that requires evidence from at least two different factor categories.
The catalog that describes the information a device can report through SNMP.
A multi-fiber connector that terminates several optical fibers in one compact connection.
A spanning-tree approach that can map groups of VLANs to different spanning-tree instances, reducing the need for a separate tree for every VLAN.
The average operating time between repairable failures, often used as a reliability measure.
The average time required to restore a service after failure. Some organizations use the same initials for mean time to repair, so read the surrounding definition.
The largest network-layer packet or link-layer payload an interface can carry without fragmentation or another accommodation.
A DNS record that identifies the mail server responsible for accepting email for a domain and includes a preference value.
Technology that evaluates users or devices before and during network access, then permits, restricts, or isolates them.
A networked storage system that provides file-level access through protocols such as SMB or NFS.
A network function that rewrites IP address information between address spaces.
A translation method that allows IPv6-only clients to communicate with IPv4 services, commonly with a DNS64 function.
A network file-sharing protocol commonly associated with Unix-like systems and network-attached storage.
Running network functions such as routing, firewalling, or load balancing as software rather than only on dedicated appliances.
The hardware or virtual adapter that connects a system to a network and supplies link-layer functions such as a MAC address.
A DNS record that identifies the authoritative name servers for a zone or delegated domain.
A protocol used to synchronize system clocks, which is important for logs, authentication, and investigations.
A security extension for NTP that authenticates time synchronization and helps resist tampering and spoofed time sources.
A DNS response indicating that the queried domain name does not exist. It is useful evidence when troubleshooting name resolution.
The unique number used to request one item from an SNMP management catalog.
The software layer that manages hardware, processes, memory, files, and system services.
A seven-layer reference model used to organize networking functions and structure troubleshooting reasoning.
A link-state interior routing protocol that calculates shortest paths from exchanged topology information and uses areas for scale.
Hardware and software that monitors or controls physical processes, equipment, and industrial operations.
A fiber troubleshooting instrument that sends light pulses and analyzes reflections to estimate the distance to breaks, bends, splices, connectors, and other optical events.
A cloud model in which the provider manages the underlying platform while the customer deploys applications and data.
A form of NAT that maps many internal connections to one public address by tracking transport-layer ports.

entries.expansion: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
entries.meaning: An industry security standard for organizations that store, process, or transmit payment-card data.
A device that distributes electrical power to rack equipment. Do not confuse it with protocol data unit in an OSI discussion.
The people, policies, services, keys, and certificates used to establish and manage public-key trust.
Supplies electrical power and Ethernet data over compatible copper cabling to devices such as access points, phones, and cameras.
A secret configured on participating systems before secure communication begins.
A time-synchronization protocol designed for greater precision than ordinary NTP in supported networks and applications.
A DNS reverse-lookup record that maps an IP address representation back to a hostname.
Classification, marking, queuing, shaping, and related policies used to manage delay, loss, and priority for different traffic.
A compact, high-density transceiver form factor commonly used for higher-speed links and breakout connections.
A protocol that centralizes authentication, authorization, and accounting for network access.
An access model that assigns permissions to job roles and then assigns users to those roles.
A Microsoft protocol for interactive remote desktop sessions.
A numbered publication in the Internet standards and engineering series. Some RFCs define standards, while others are informational.
A technology that uses radio signals to identify tags, cards, assets, or devices.
A distance-vector interior routing protocol that uses hop count and has limited scale compared with modern alternatives.
A registered-jack designation used in connector names. Network cabling commonly uses the familiar RJ45-style modular connector.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured backward in time from a disruption.
A faster-converging evolution of spanning tree that moves switch ports through simplified states after topology changes.
The maximum acceptable time for restoring a service after disruption. The phrase return to operations can be a useful memory cue, but the Security+ term is Recovery Time Objective.
Carries real-time audio or video media, commonly using negotiated UDP ports while a signaling protocol such as SIP manages the session.
The receive side of a link, optic, or interface. Transposed transmit and receive paths can prevent link establishment.
A cloud model in which the provider operates the application while the customer manages users, data, and selected configuration.
An XML-based standard used to exchange authentication and authorization assertions, commonly for federation and single sign-on.
A dedicated storage network that presents block-level storage to servers, commonly using Fibre Channel or iSCSI.
Delivers networking and security controls through cloud services so users and branch locations receive consistent protection wherever they connect.
A push-pull fiber connector larger than LC and still found in patch panels, carrier facilities, and older installations.
Systems that monitor and control industrial processes across distributed locations.
A secure file-copy method that uses SSH for protected transport and authentication.
A centrally managed WAN architecture that selects paths and applies policy across multiple links.
A network architecture that separates centralized control logic from packet forwarding.
A modular transceiver form factor used for copper or fiber links at supported speeds and distances.
A secure file-transfer protocol that runs over SSH. It is different from FTPS.
A platform that collects, correlates, searches, and alerts on logs and security events.
A signaling protocol used to establish, modify, and end voice or multimedia sessions; the media commonly travels separately over RTP.
A contract or commitment that defines measurable service expectations such as uptime and response times.
An IPv6 mechanism that lets a host form an address from router-advertisement information without a stateful address lease.
A protocol used for shared files, printers, and related services, especially in Windows environments.
The standard protocol for sending and relaying email.
SMTP protected with TLS. The term may refer to implicit TLS or, informally, to secure mail submission depending on context.
Lets monitoring software request status and counters from network devices and receive event notifications.
The DNS record that identifies key authority and timing information for a zone, including the primary server and serial number.
A language used to create, query, and manage relational databases.
Cloud-delivered security services such as secure web access, cloud access security, and zero-trust access without the WAN transport portion of SASE.
A protocol for encrypted remote administration, command execution, tunneling, and file transfer.
The human-readable wireless network name advertised or configured for a Wi-Fi service.
A retired predecessor to TLS. Modern secure services should negotiate supported TLS versions rather than legacy SSL.
An identity arrangement that lets a user authenticate once and access multiple connected services.
A bayonet-style fiber connector used in some legacy campus, industrial, and test environments.
Copper cabling with shielding that helps reduce electromagnetic interference when correctly selected, grounded, and installed.
A Layer 2 loop-prevention protocol that selects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths until they are needed.
A logical Layer 3 interface associated with a VLAN, used for management or inter-VLAN routing on a multilayer switch.
A TCP control flag used when establishing a connection. A client normally begins the handshake with SYN and expects a SYN-ACK response.

entries.expansion: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
entries.meaning: A protocol commonly used for centralized administration access to network devices, with separate authentication, authorization, and accounting functions.
A connection-oriented transport protocol that provides ordered delivery, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control.
The practical protocol suite built around IP addressing and transports such as TCP and UDP, rather than a single protocol.
A copper-cabling troubleshooting instrument that measures reflected electrical signals to estimate the distance to an open, short, or impedance change.
A minimal UDP file-transfer protocol without the authentication and features of FTP or SFTP, often used for boot or configuration files.
A protocol that protects network communication with encryption, integrity, and certificate-based authentication.
A field that limits how many routed hops an IP packet can traverse, preventing packets from circulating indefinitely.
The transmit side of a link, optic, or interface. A TX/RX reversal or incompatible optic can prevent communication.
A DNS record containing text data, commonly used for domain verification and email-policy information.
A connectionless transport protocol with low overhead and no built-in delivery guarantee.
A battery-backed device that supplies short-term power and conditions electricity during an outage or fluctuation.
A URI that identifies a resource by location and access method.
A standard for connecting peripherals, storage, power, and data interfaces.
A security appliance that combines several controls such as firewalling, intrusion prevention, filtering, and malware protection.
Copper twisted-pair cabling without an overall shield, widely used for Ethernet in ordinary office environments.
A fiber tool that sends visible light through a strand to help identify fibers and reveal some nearby breaks or severe bends.
A logical IP address associated with a redundant gateway, load balancer, cluster, or service rather than one fixed interface.
A logical Layer 2 network segment created on switching infrastructure.
Using different prefix lengths within an address plan so each subnet receives an appropriately sized block.
Voice and related signaling carried over IP networks, with quality affected by latency, jitter, loss, and prioritization.
A logically isolated cloud network in which customers define subnets, routes, and security controls.
An encrypted tunnel that protects traffic across an untrusted network.
An overlay encapsulation that carries Layer 2 segments across a Layer 3 underlay using a larger logical segment identifier.
A network that connects systems across large geographic areas or multiple sites.
A local network that uses Wi-Fi radio links instead of only wired Ethernet connections.
A family of Wi-Fi security standards. WPA2 and WPA3 provide stronger modern protections than the original WPA design.
A Wi-Fi security generation that commonly uses AES-based protection and supports personal or enterprise authentication.
A newer Wi-Fi security generation with stronger modern protections than WPA2, including improved personal-mode authentication when supported.
A convenience method for enrolling devices in a Wi-Fi network. PIN-based WPS has well-known security concerns and is often disabled.
An architecture that continuously evaluates identity, device, resource, and policy signals instead of trusting a user because of network location.
